lead: An inverter turns DC into AC by switching the load between two voltage rails. In single-phase square-wave operation the output is not a sine: it is a rectangular wave whose height is fixed by the DC bus. The half-bridge uses two switches and a split capacitor bus; the full bridge uses four switches and gives twice the voltage. These circuits appear in small UPS units, solar microinverters and variable-speed drives, and they are the base on which PWM is built.
prereq: You need: Unit 1 for the IGBT, its anti-parallel diode and switching times, and Unit 3 for the idea of a switched-mode source.

blocks.text: The half-bridge has two switches, S1 on top and S2 below, in series across the DC bus V<sub>dc</sub>. Two equal capacitors C1 and C2 also sit across the bus, and their midpoint is the circuit reference. The top rail is then +V<sub>dc</sub>/2 and the bottom rail is −V<sub>dc</sub>/2.

S1 on connects the load to +V<sub>dc</sub>/2; S2 on connects it to −V<sub>dc</sub>/2. Each switch conducts for 180° of the output cycle. The load voltage is a square wave of amplitude V<sub>dc</sub>/2, so its rms value is V<sub>dc</sub>/2. The fundamental peak is 2V<sub>dc</sub>/π.

blocks.where: v<sub>o</sub> is the load voltage; V<sub>dc</sub> is the DC bus; V<sub>rms</sub> is the root-mean-square output; V<sub>1,peak</sub> is the peak of the fundamental.

blocks.text: C1 and C2 must hold the midpoint steady while carrying the load's alternating current. Before S2 turns on, S1 must be off for a short dead time, and the reverse for the other half cycle. If both conduct together, the bus is shorted. Some syllabi call this a split-supply inverter.

sections.h3: Full bridge: four switches, full voltage

blocks.text: The full bridge, or H-bridge, has four switches in two legs. Leg A is S1 above S2; leg B is S3 above S4. The load sits between the midpoints. S1 and S4 conduct together for the positive half cycle; S2 and S3 conduct together for the negative half cycle. Each device conducts for 180°. The load voltage is +V<sub>dc</sub> for one half cycle and −V<sub>dc</sub> for the other, so its rms value is V<sub>dc</sub>.

blocks.where: ω = 2πf; f is the output frequency in hertz; n = 1, 3, 5, … is the harmonic order. The peak of the fundamental is 4V<sub>dc</sub>/π. The nth harmonic peak is 4V<sub>dc</sub>/(nπ), which is 1/n of the fundamental.

blocks.text: Even harmonics and DC are zero because the wave has half-wave symmetry. With a pure resistor, the current is the same square wave as the voltage. With an R-L load, the current is smoother and lags; when a switch turns off, the load current continues through the anti-parallel diode of the other switch and returns energy to the bus. The output voltage remains a square wave, but the current is not.

The square wave's rms value is V<sub>dc</sub> for the full bridge and V<sub>dc</sub>/2 for the half-bridge. The nth harmonic rms is 4V<sub>dc</sub>/(nπ√2) for the full bridge, with n odd. The fundamental carries most of the power; the 3rd, 5th and 7th cause extra heating and torque ripple.

blocks.where: V<sub>n,rms</sub> is the rms of the nth harmonic of a full-bridge square wave.

blocks.text: Dead time is the short interval when both switches of one leg are off. It prevents shoot-through, a direct short of the DC bus. Dead time slightly lowers the fundamental and adds low-order distortion, so it is kept small. To control the fundamental without changing Vdc, see Chapter 4.3.

figure.caption: The DC bus feeds two legs; the load between their midpoints sees ±300 V. Notice that each leg has two switches, and only one switch per leg is on at a time.

spec.title: Single-phase full bridge
spec.aria: A 300 V DC bus feeds two switch legs, and the load between their midpoints sees a ±300 V square wave.

examples.question: A single-phase full bridge runs from V<sub>dc</sub> = 300 V and feeds a 20 Ω resistor at 50 Hz in square-wave mode. Find (a) the rms output voltage, (b) the output power, (c) the rms of the fundamental and its power, (d) the rms of the third harmonic.
steps: Full-bridge square wave: amplitude A = V<sub>dc</sub> = 300 V. The wave is at +300 V or −300 V all the time; f = 50 Hz sets the fundamental frequency only.
examples.answer: The full bridge gives 300 V rms, 4500 W total, fundamental 270.09 V rms (3647.56 W) and third harmonic 90.03 V rms.
examples.check:
import math
Vdc = 300.0
R = 20.0
Vrms = Vdc
P = Vrms**2 / R
V1p = 4 * Vdc / math.pi
V1rms = V1p / math.sqrt(2)
P1 = V1rms**2 / R
V3p = V1p / 3
V3rms = V3p / math.sqrt(2)
for x in (Vrms, P, V1p, V1rms, P1, V3p, V3rms):
    print(round(x, 2))

traps: Half-bridge amplitude is V<sub>dc</sub>/2, not V<sub>dc</sub>; its rms is V<sub>dc</sub>/2, while the full bridge gives V<sub>dc</sub>.
If both switches in one leg are on together, the DC bus is shorted: this is shoot-through. Dead time prevents it.
The fundamental peak is 4V<sub>dc</sub>/π for a full bridge, not V<sub>dc</sub>. The nth harmonic is 1/n of that, not 1/n².
With an R-L load the output voltage is still a square wave; the current is smoother. Do not draw the current as a square wave.
180° conduction means each device is on for half the cycle. 120° conduction belongs to the three-phase inverter in Chapter 4.2.

quiz.q: What is the peak amplitude of the load voltage in a single-phase half-bridge inverter with bus V<sub>dc</sub>?
Why does the full-bridge square wave have no even harmonics?
quiz.a: It has half-wave symmetry: v(t) = −v(t + T/2), so even terms cancel.

quiz.q: A full bridge has V<sub>dc</sub> = 200 V and R = 10 Ω. Find the rms fundamental voltage and the power it delivers.
Why are anti-parallel diodes needed with an R-L load even if the switches are IGBTs?
quiz.a: Load current cannot change instantly. When a switch turns off, the diode provides a path and returns stored inductive energy to the DC bus; without it, voltage spikes can destroy the switch.

quiz.q: A half-bridge runs from V<sub>dc</sub> = 400 V. Find the rms output and the fundamental peak and rms.
quiz.a: rms = 200 V; V<sub>1,peak</sub> = 2×400/π = 254.65 V; V<sub>1,rms</sub> = 180.06 V.

quiz.q: What is shoot-through and how is it prevented?
quiz.a: Both switches of one leg conduct, shorting the DC bus. Insert dead time: turn one off and wait before turning the other on.

beyond: Not for the exam. Commercial single-phase inverters add current control, dead-time compensation and filtering so the output approaches a sine. Wide-band-gap SiC and GaN switches allow higher switching frequencies and smaller filters, but they make dead-time and layout parasitics more critical. Search for dead-time distortion, unipolar PWM and SiC half-bridge modules.
